title: 140 Gastrointestinal parasite prevalence and anthelmintic efficacy on beef cattle farms in Kentucky
content:
Abstract
The objective of this study was to evaluate the prevalence of gastrointestinal parasites in Kentucky beef cattle and assess the efficacy of anthelmintic products. Fecal samples were collected in two seasons (spring & fall) and classified as either mature cows or growing cattle. Fecal samples were shipped to a commercial laboratory and a modified Wisconsin sugar floatation method was used to determine total fecal egg count (FEC) and the incidence of specific parasites in a 3-gram sample. Ordinal classifications were assigned to parasites to categorize low, medium, or high incidences of each within a sample. Parasite prevalence was calculated from fecal samples collected from 180 groups of animals before anthelmintic application (PRE). Prevalence data were evaluated using PROC FREQ in SAS (9.4). The Fecal Egg Count Reduction (FECR) Test approach was used to assess anthelmintic efficacy based on the reduction of gastrointestinal parasites between fecal samples randomly collected before (PRE) and 14 days after (POST) anthelmintic treatment. To qualify for statistical analysis, groups required at least 18 animals of the same age class with an average PRE FEC of at least 10 eggs per sample resulting in 35 mature cow and 44 growing cattle groups being included. Samples were further separated by anthelmintic product used: macrocyclic lactone (ML), benzimidazole (Benz), or a combination (Combo). To assess FECR of specific parasites, ordinal classifications were transformed using the total FEC to estimate numeric occurrence within each sample. The eggCounts package in R (4.4.1) was used to analyze qualifying group FECR data and parasite FECR with alpha set to 0.10. Only stomach worms and Cooperia were sufficiently represented for statistical analysis. Stomach worms and Cooperia were detected in 60% and 22% of samples from mature cows and 78% and 74% of samples from growing animals, respectively. In groups treated with ML, FECR was estimated at 74% and 64% for mature cows and growing cattle, respectively. Benz groups had an estimated FECR of 99% for mature cows and 99% for growing cattle. Estimations for mature cow and growing cattle FECR were 95% and 99%, respectively, for Combo groups. Estimated FECR of stomach worms in samples from mature cows treated with ML, Benz, and Combo was 67%, 84%, and 93%, respectively, whereas FECR of Cooperia was 38%, 88%, and 97%, respectively. Growing cattle treated with ML, Benz, and Combo had estimated FECR for stomach worms of 78%, 99%, and 99%, respectively, whereas FECR of Cooperia was 40%, 100%, and 99%, respectively. Growing cattle had greater prevalence of fecal eggs. The use of ML alone appears to result in lower FECR when compared to the use of Benz or Combo. Due to limited groups of Benz and Combo, additional studies are warranted.
